opus-5.5.text:
Well, the virtual cell is something I've been dreaming about for, honestly, decades. It's one of my longest-held ambitions, going back to my undergrad days. The idea is to build a simulation of a living cell that's accurate enough that you could run experiments in silico and have the predictions hold up when you go and check them in the wet lab.

The way I think about building it is bottom-up, layer by layer. AlphaFold was really the first piece: understanding the static structure of proteins. But biology isn't static. So the next steps are about interactions and dynamics: how proteins bind to each other, to DNA, to RNA, to small molecules. That's what we've been pushing on with things like AlphaFold 3, moving from individual structures to complexes and interactions. Then you go up a level to pathways, then to whole systems within the cell, and eventually to the full cell.

I think the right first target is something like a yeast cell. It's a relatively simple eukaryotic organism, extremely well studied, and we have a huge amount of experimental data on it. If you could model a yeast cell faithfully, predicting how it responds to a perturbation like knocking out a gene or adding a compound, that would be a remarkable proof of concept. Then you'd scale up toward human cells.

The key insight, I think, is that you don't need to simulate every atom from first principles. That would be computationally intractable. Instead you use learned models that capture the essential behavior at each level of abstraction, and you stitch them together. It's a bit like how we approached Go or protein folding: find the right representation, learn from data, and let the model discover the patterns that are too complex for us to write down by hand.

There's also a really important interplay with experimental biology. The simulation generates hypotheses, the lab tests them, and that data feeds back into the model. Over time you'd hope the virtual cell becomes so good that it massively accelerates drug discovery and our basic understanding of disease. Instead of ten years and billions of dollars to find a drug, maybe you can do a lot of that search computationally first.

I'd say we're maybe a decade away from something really convincing, possibly sooner given how fast things are moving. But to me it's one of the most exciting applications of AI there is, because it gets at the fundamental question of what life actually is and how it works.

r001.rationale: It proposes running experiments in silico, then checking the predictions in the wet lab.

r002.rationale: It names yeast as a target because it is relatively simple, well studied, and data rich; it does not say a single yeast cell is a complete organism.

r003.rationale: It contrasts static protein structures with biology’s interactions and dynamics, including binding among proteins, DNA, RNA, and small molecules.

r004.rationale: It explicitly places pathways after molecular interactions and before whole-cell modeling.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think of it as the natural next step after AlphaFold. AlphaFold gave us the static structure of a protein, and that's been incredibly useful, but a cell isn't static. It's this enormously complex dynamic system, with thousands of proteins interacting, pathways switching on and off, things happening across many different time scales and length scales. So the question is, can we build a model that captures that dynamics well enough that you could do experiments in silico, perturb the system, knock out a gene or add a drug, and get a reliable prediction of what happens?

The way I envision building it is in stages, a bit like how we approached the protein problem. You start with the pieces we already understand reasonably well, proteins, their interactions, complexes, and then you build up to pathways, to organelles, and eventually to something like a whole simple cell, maybe a yeast cell to begin with. And I don't think you do it purely from first principles, simulating every atom, that's computationally hopeless. You do it with learned models, trained on the huge amounts of experimental data that are now available, single-cell sequencing, imaging, proteomics, all of that. The learning system finds the right level of abstraction, the way AlphaFold found the right abstraction for folding without simulating physics directly.

The other crucial piece is the loop with the wet lab. You make predictions, test the ones where the model is most uncertain, feed the results back in. That's where I think AI really changes the pace of science, because it tells you which experiments are most informative. And if we get there, even a partially faithful virtual cell, you could compress years of drug discovery into months, because you'd understand mechanism, not just correlation. It's one of those grand challenges that I think is actually tractable now, in a way it wasn't five years ago.

r001.rationale: It proposes in-silico experiments and perturbations, then testing informative predictions in the wet lab.

r002.rationale: It names yeast as a possible starting cell but does not say a yeast cell is a complete organism or give that as the reason.

r003.rationale: It contrasts AlphaFold’s static protein structure with the dynamic cell, emphasizing interacting proteins and changing pathways.

r004.rationale: It describes building from proteins and their interactions to pathways, then organelles and a whole cell.

astra-6.text:
I think of Virtual Cell as a kind of virtual laboratory. The ambition is to build a model of a cell that’s useful enough that you can ask: What happens if I knock out this gene, or introduce this molecule? Can we predict how the cell responds, and then test that prediction experimentally?

The challenge is that knowing the structures of the proteins is only part of the story. You need to understand how they interact, how those interactions change over time, and how they depend on the state of the cell. There are many different scales involved, from molecular events to the behavior of the whole system.

So I would approach it incrementally. Start with a particular type of cell and a constrained set of behaviors. Combine learned models with what we know about the underlying physics and biology, and then establish a very tight loop with experiments. The model makes a prediction, you test it, and the discrepancy tells you what to investigate next.

You probably don’t want to simulate every atom to capture every useful aspect of a cell. The key scientific question is: What level of abstraction preserves the behavior you care about? If we can get that right, even an imperfect virtual cell could be enormously useful for understanding disease and designing new medicines.

r001.rationale: The response proposes using the virtual cell to predict outcomes of gene knockouts or molecule introductions, then testing those predictions experimentally.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify yeast as a simulation target or give the reason that a yeast cell is a complete organism.

r003.rationale: It says protein structures are only part of the story and emphasizes understanding how proteins interact and how those interactions change over time.

r004.rationale: The response does not propose modeling a whole biological pathway as an intermediate stage between pairwise interactions and an entire cell.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the way to approach it is to build up from the components, but always keep the whole system in view. A cell isn’t just a collection of proteins. It’s a dynamic system: those proteins interact, genes are switched on and off, molecules move between compartments, and all of that changes over time.

So you’d want models at different levels of abstraction. You can’t simulate every atom over biologically meaningful timescales, so the question becomes: which details do you need to preserve to predict the behavior you care about? You might model some interactions in great detail and represent other processes more approximately.

The crucial thing would be to make it an experimental loop. The model predicts what happens if you knock out a gene or introduce a molecule; you do that experiment in a real cell, compare the results, and use the discrepancy to improve the model. Ideally, it also tells you which experiment would be most informative to do next.

I’d start with a constrained system and a well-defined set of behaviors, rather than claim we could capture everything immediately. But if we could get to a model that reliably predicts how a cell responds to interventions, that would be tremendously useful for understanding disease and designing medicines. That’s the ambition: a simulation you can actually do science with.

r001.rationale: The response proposes modeling interventions, testing the predictions in real cells, and using the comparison to improve the model—an experimental loop for exploring possibilities before wet-lab validation.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify yeast or give a reason to simulate it.

r003.rationale: It describes the cell as a dynamic system whose proteins interact and emphasizes predicting behavior over time, locating behavior in interactions rather than protein structure alone.

r004.rationale: The response discusses models at different abstraction levels but does not propose modeling a whole pathway as an intermediate stage between pairwise interactions and the entire cell.
